explanations.explanation: Eight years, friend. Acts 9:33 says Aeneas had been paralyzed and bedridden that long. I think that's a heavy stretch of time. Eight is the number to hold onto.

Twelve is a number that shows up in other stories, but this one gives a different count. The text says Aeneas had been paralyzed and bedridden for eight years. It's an easy mix-up, friend. Eight is the one to hold onto here.

Thirty-eight belongs to a different man in a different story (John 5:5). Here the text says Aeneas had been paralyzed and bedridden for eight years. Eight is already plenty long, friend. Nobody needs thirty extra years to feel how heavy that is.
That's it, baker. Peter says, “Aeneas… Jesus Christ heals you!” Peter doesn't take the credit. He points straight at the One doing the healing.
I love the confidence, but Peter doesn't claim it. He tells Aeneas, “Jesus Christ heals you!” Peter is the one talking, but he points away from himself. Peter hands the credit right over to Jesus.

The saints are the ones Peter came to visit, friend (Acts 9:32). But when he speaks to Aeneas, he says, “Jesus Christ heals you!” The healing is credited to Jesus, not to the saints. They aren't the ones Peter names.
Yes, baker. Peter says, “Get up and put away your mat.” After eight years of lying down, that's quite a command. And the text says Aeneas got up immediately.
Lie still? That's the opposite of what Peter says, friend. He tells Aeneas, “Get up and put away your mat.” And the text says Aeneas got up immediately.
No waiting around in this one, friend. Peter says, “Get up and put away your mat.” That's a command to move, not to hang about. And the text says Aeneas got up immediately.
It's tempting, friend. After eight years in bed, you'd expect a slow, wobbly start. But the text says, “Immediately Aeneas got up…” No recovery days are mentioned, and no wobbling either.
Right, baker. The text says, “Immediately Aeneas got up…” No waiting period is mentioned at all. After eight years in bed, he's on his feet at once.

That's the one, baker. The text says all who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord. The whole area saw Aeneas after he got up. It's hard to argue with what they saw: a man who'd been bedridden for eight years, and he got up.

explanations.answer: They run Peter out of town
explanations.explanation: Nobody chases Peter anywhere in this passage, friend. The people of Lydda and Sharon saw Aeneas up and turned to the Lord. That's about as far from running someone out of town as you can get. They're drawn in, not pushed out.

explanations.answer: They bring Peter more sick people
explanations.explanation: That sounds like what a crowd might do, friend, but the text doesn't say it. It says all who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw Aeneas and turned to the Lord. Their response was to turn to the Lord, and the passage doesn't mention a line of sick people.
Yes, baker. Acts 9:36 says Dorcas, a disciple in Joppa, was always occupied with works of kindness and charity. Always. Not once in a while. I'd love that on my own handle.

Tent making comes up in another story, about Paul and his friends (Acts 18:3). Dorcas isn't described that way. The text says she was always occupied with works of kindness and charity. Her whole schedule was one big good deed.

Purple cloth belongs to Lydia, a seller of purple cloth in another story (Acts 16:14). Dorcas has a different calling here. The text says she was always occupied with works of kindness and charity. Same cloth neighborhood, friend, different story.

I see why you'd say it, friend, since a tomb is what many of us picture. But the text says her body was washed and placed in an upper room. No tomb is mentioned in this passage. It's a quieter detail that matters when Peter walks in.
Right, baker. The text says her body was washed and placed in an upper room. A tomb outside the city never comes up. That upper room is where Peter goes later.
That's it, baker. The disciples sent two men to urge Peter, “Come to us without delay.” They sent people to ask him in person. I think they wanted Peter there as fast as he could manage.
They don't ask for long-distance prayer, friend. The two men urge Peter, “Come to us without delay.” They want him to come to them. And Peter gets up and goes with them.

explanations.answer: Come once his work is done
explanations.explanation: That's pretty much the opposite, friend. The two men say, “Come to us without delay.” No waiting for Peter to finish up. The message was to come right away, and Peter got up and went with them.

Right, baker. The widows were weeping and showing Peter the tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was still with them. That's a closet full of her kindness. They don't just tell Peter about her. They hold it up for him to see.
Letters would make sense, friend, but the text doesn't mention any. The widows showed Peter the tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made. I think those clothes said plenty.

No coins turn up in this scene, friend. The widows, still weeping, show Peter the tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made. They show what her hands made, not what she saved. It's a simple, touching detail.
Yes, baker. After sending everyone out, Peter knelt down and prayed. It's the first thing he does in that quiet room. Then he turns toward her body and speaks.
The widows were the ones weeping, friend. Peter sent them all out, then knelt down and prayed. The text doesn't say he wept. Kneeling and praying is what it records.
Peter doesn't just stand around waiting, friend. The text says he knelt down and prayed. Only after that does he turn toward her body and speak. Prayer comes first.
That's right, baker. After he prays, Peter turns toward her body and says, “Tabitha, get up!” He speaks right to her. That's a bold thing to say in a quiet room.
I think the quiet room fooled you, friend. The text says Peter, turning toward her body, said, “Tabitha, get up!” He speaks right to her, and the same verse says she opens her eyes.
Yes, baker. The text says she opened her eyes, and seeing Peter, she sat up. First the eyes open, then she sits up. Before that, Peter had knelt down and prayed.
She doesn't call anyone, friend, at least not in the text. It says she opened her eyes, and seeing Peter, she sat up. The widows were sent out of the room earlier. Peter calls them in later.

That's a fair thing to wonder, friend, but the text doesn't give her a single word here. She opened her eyes, and seeing Peter, she sat up. I think we can safely bet it was a surprise for everybody. The text records only what she does.
Right, baker. Peter called the saints and widows and presented her to them alive. Those are the same widows who had been standing around weeping. Now they see her alive.
No priests show up in this scene, friend. Peter called the saints and widows and presented Dorcas to them alive. The widows are the ones who had been standing around weeping.
No soldiers in this room, friend. The text says Peter called the saints and widows and presented her to them alive. The widows are the ones who had been showing Peter the clothing Dorcas made.
Yes, baker. The text says it became known all over Joppa, and many people believed in the Lord. The news spread and faith spread with it. That's a ripple that started in one upper room.
I'd flip that one around, friend. The text says this became known all over Joppa, and many people believed in the Lord. The news doesn't fizzle out. It travels, and many believe.
That's right, baker. The text says Peter stayed for several days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon. A tanner is someone who works with animal hides. Peter is the guest here, and Simon is the host.

Levi is a tax collector in the Gospel of Luke (Luke 5:27), friend. In this passage, the text says Peter stayed with a tanner named Simon. A tanner works with animal hides, not tax records. It's a fair mix-up, but the host is Simon.

Aquila is a tentmaker in a different story (Acts 18:2-3). Here the text says Peter stayed for several days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon. A tanner works with animal hides, friend. The host here is Simon, not Aquila.
